q: Heat is the form of energy that can be transferred from one system to another as a result of temperature difference.
e: True. Match the two temperatures and net heat flow stops. Heat is energy that flows from a hotter system to a colder one. A temperature difference is the cause, not a mass or volume gap.

q: Heat is the form of energy that can be transferred from one system to another as a result of pressure difference.
e: False. Heat is energy that flows because of a temperature difference. A pressure difference can push fluid around, but that is not the definition of heat. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow.

q: Heat transfer and thermodynamics are two complementary branches of science.
e: True. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. Thermodynamics maps equilibrium states involving heat and work. Heat transfer then asks how energy actually flows.

q: Heat transfer and thermodynamics are two unrelated branches of science.
e: False. Heat transfer and thermodynamics are complementary, not unrelated. Thermodynamics maps equilibrium energy and work. Heat transfer then describes how thermal energy actually moves.

q: Heat transfer is a discipline of thermal engineering that concerns the generation, use, conversion, and exchange of thermal energy between systems.
e: True. Heat transfer is the thermal-engineering study of generating, using, converting and exchanging thermal energy. That is a flow problem, not just a balance sheet of U. Thermodynamics sits beside it as the equilibrium partner.

q: Thermodynamics deals with equilibrium states by outlining the relationship between energy and work.
e: True. Thermodynamics maps equilibrium states and how energy links to work. It does not track the rate of heat flow through a wall. Heat transfer is the complementary flow subject.

q: Thermodynamics deals with non-equilibrium states by outlining the relationship between energy and work.
e: False. Thermodynamics deals with equilibrium states and the link between energy and work. Non-equilibrium flow is the heat-transfer side of the story. Mix the two and the zeroth-law idea of temperature falls apart.

q: One of the basic requirements for heat transfer is the presence of a temperature difference.
e: True. Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow.

q: There can be no net heat transfer between two systems that are at the same temperature.
e: True. Only a temperature gap drives a net current. Systems at the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium. Net heat transfer between them is zero.

q: There can be maximum net heat transfer between two systems that are at the same temperature.
e: False. Two systems at the same temperature have no net heat transfer. A temperature difference is the basic requirement. Same temperature is thermal equilibrium, not a heat flood.

q: There are three basic ways of heat transfer; namely, heat conduction, heat convection and heat radiation.
e: True. The three heat-transfer modes are conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction is neighbour vibration, convection is bulk fluid motion, radiation is electromagnetic waves. Keep those three jobs separate.

q: In fluids, heat is mainly transferred by convection, in which the motion of the fluid itself carries heat from one place to another.
e: True. In fluids the main heat carrier is convection, because the fluid itself moves. Hot, less dense fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks. Conduction in a solid does not need that bulk current.

q: In fluids, heat is mainly transferred by conduction, in which the motion of the fluid itself carries heat from one place to another.
e: False. In fluids the main carrier is convection, because the fluid itself moves. Conduction is neighbour-to-neighbour vibration without bulk flow. The motion clause in this statement already names convection.

q: In solid, heat is transferred by conduction process in which heat energy is transferred among the adjacent parts of the material without the motion of the material itself.
e: True. Conduction spreads energy through adjacent parts of the material. Each vibrating neighbour feeds the next. Distant, disconnected regions do not conduct to each other directly.

q: The third way to transfer heat energy is by radiation process in the form of electromagnetic waves.
e: True. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not attenuate the wave. Mechanical or sound waves are a different family. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves.

q: The third way to transfer heat energy is by radiation process in the form of mechanical waves.
e: False. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves, not mechanical waves. Mechanical waves need a material medium. Radiation can cross vacuum at the speed of light.

q: The individual parts of a medium do not move whole in heat conduction.
e: True. That is why a metal poker can heat your hand while the rod stays put. In conduction the bulk of the medium does not move as a whole. Energy is handed along adjacent parts.

q: Heat energy is transferred by successive distribution among the adjacent parts in heat conduction.
e: True. Each vibrating neighbour feeds the next. Distant, disconnected regions do not conduct to each other directly. Conduction spreads energy through adjacent parts of the material.

q: When heat is transferred via conduction, heat energy is transferred internally by vibrations of atoms and molecules.
e: True. Free protons do not stream through the lattice as a heat current. Conduction inside matter is internal vibrations of atoms and molecules. Metals add a sea of free electrons on top of that.

q: When heat is transferred via conduction, heat energy is transferred internally by the flow of free protons.
e: False. Conduction inside a solid is vibrations of atoms and molecules, plus free electrons in metals. Free protons are locked in nuclei and do not stream through the lattice as a heat current.

q: Metals have many free electrons.
e: True. Metals have many free electrons. Those electrons can drift and carry thermal energy, so metals are good heat conductors. Bound electrons locked to one ion cannot roam like that.

q: Since these free electrons can carry heat, metals are generally very good conductors of heat.
e: True. Copper and silver are the textbook high-k examples. Wood, rubber and styrofoam sit at the poor-conductor end. Metals have many free electrons.

q: Since these free electrons can carry heat, metals are generally very poor conductors of heat.
e: False. Those free electrons make metals generally very good heat conductors. Copper and silver run high thermal conductivity for the same reason they run high electrical conductivity. Rubber and wood sit at the poor-conductor end.

q: The rate of heat conduction through a material of cross-sectional area $A$ is proportional to the temperature difference $\Delta T$.
e: True. Steeper drop, larger heat current. Conduction rate is proportional to temperature difference Delta T. It is inversely proportional to thickness, not to Delta T.

q: The rate of heat conduction through a material of cross-sectional area $A$ is inversely proportional to the temperature difference $\Delta T$.
e: False. Conduction rate rises with temperature difference; it is proportional to Delta T, not inversely. Thickness l is the quantity that sits in the denominator. Fourier's H = k A Delta T / l makes that plain.

q: The rate of heat conduction through a material is inversely proportional to the thickness $l$ of the material.
e: True. Fourier's formula H = k A Delta T / l is that statement in symbols. Heat current through a slab is inversely proportional to thickness l. A thinner wall, larger area, or larger Delta T raises H.

q: The heat transfer or conduction rate $H$ is $H = kA \frac{T_2 - T_1}{l}$.
e: True. Conduction hands energy to neighbouring atoms while the bulk stays put. Metals add free electrons on top of those vibrations. A rigid solid can conduct; it cannot convect.

q: In the heat conduction formula, $k$ is the thermal conductivity of the material, which is a measure of the ability of a material to conduct heat.
e: True. k is thermal conductivity, a measure of how well the material conducts heat. SI unit is W m^-1 K^-1. Large k is a conductor; small k is an insulator.

q: In SI units, $k$ is watt per metre per kelvin ($W m^{-1} K^{-1}$).
e: True. units and watt have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of units would describe a different law.

q: In SI units, $k$ is watt per metre squared per kelvin ($W m^{-2} K^{-1}$).
e: False. Thermal conductivity k is watt per metre per kelvin, W m^-1 K^-1. Watt per metre squared per kelvin is the convection coefficient q. Heat flux itself is watt per metre squared.

q: The ratio $\frac{T_2 - T_1}{l}$ is called temperature gradient.
e: True. Temperature gradient is (T2 - T1)/l, the temperature drop per unit thickness. Fourier says heat flux density is proportional to that gradient. The minus sign in the local law means T falls as x increases along the flow.

q: This mathematical model of heat conduction was first formulated by the French physicist Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier in his Fourier's law of heat conduction.
e: True. Fourier wrote the conduction law that heat flux follows the temperature gradient. The French physicist Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier gave that mathematical model. Newton's law of cooling is the convection cousin, not this solid-slab law.

q: Fourier's law of heat conduction states that the rate of heat flow per unit area (heat flux density) is proportional to the magnitude of temperature gradient.
e: True. Thermal conductivity is heat transfer per unit area per unit temperature gradient. That is why k's unit is W m^-1 K^-1. Drop the extra metre and you have mixed k with the convection coefficient.

q: Fourier's law of heat conduction states that the rate of heat flow per unit area is inversely proportional to the magnitude of temperature gradient.
e: False. Fourier's law says heat flux density is proportional to the temperature gradient, not inversely. Heat runs down the gradient, which is why the differential form carries a minus sign. Steeper gradient, larger flux.

q: In Fourier's law, the negative sign indicates that temperature $T$ must decrease as distance $x$ increases.
e: True. The minus sign in Fourier's local law says temperature must decrease as distance x increases along the heat flow. Heat runs down the gradient. A plus sign would send heat toward the hot end, which is backwards.

q: In the SI units, heat flux density is watt per metre squared ($W m^{-2}$) and heat current is watt ($W$).
e: True. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body.

q: The thermal conductivity of a material can be defined as the rate of heat transfer per unit area per unit temperature gradient.
e: True. Drop the extra metre and you have mixed k with the convection coefficient. Temperature gradient is (T2 - T1)/l, the temperature drop per unit thickness. Fourier says heat flux density is proportional to that gradient.

q: A high value for thermal conductivity indicates that the material is a poor thermal conductor or thermal insulator.
e: False. High k means a good thermal conductor. Low k means a poor conductor or insulator. Copper is high-k; styrofoam is low-k.

q: A low value for thermal conductivity indicates that the material is a poor thermal conductor or thermal insulator.
e: True. High k is the opposite, a thermal conductor. Rubber, wood and styrofoam are the low-k examples. Low thermal conductivity means a poor conductor, a thermal insulator.

q: Materials such as copper and silver that are good electric conductors are also good heat conductors, and have high values of thermal conductivity.
e: True. That pairing is a useful metal rule, not a law for every insulator. Copper and silver are good electric conductors and good heat conductors, so their k is high. The same free electrons carry charge and heat.

q: Materials such as rubber, wood, and styrofoam are poor conductors of heat and have low conductivity values.
e: True. They make good thermal insulators. Do not file them next to copper. Rubber, wood and styrofoam are poor heat conductors with low k.

q: Heat convection is the flow of heat through a fluid from places of higher temperature to places of lower temperature by movement of the fluid itself.
e: True. Buoyancy drives natural convection because hot fluid is less dense. A solid cannot run this current. Convection is heat flow through a fluid by movement of the fluid itself, from hotter places to colder places.

q: Heat convection is the flow of heat through a solid from places of higher temperature to places of lower temperature by movement of the material itself.
e: False. Convection is heat carried by a moving fluid, never by a rigid solid. In a solid the bulk does not circulate. That solid-path process is conduction.

q: In heat convection, the transfer of energy occurs between an object and its environment due to fluid motion.
e: True. Convection transfers energy between an object and its surroundings because the fluid is in motion. Forced fans and natural buoyancy are both fluid motion. Vibration without bulk flow is conduction.

q: Convection currents are set up in the fluid because the hotter part of the fluid is not as dense as the cooler part.
e: True. That current never starts inside a rigid solid. Convection is heat carried by the fluid itself as it circulates. Hot fluid is less dense, so buoyancy lifts it.

q: Convection currents are set up in the fluid because the hotter part of the fluid is denser than the cooler part.
e: False. Hot fluid is less dense, so buoyancy lifts it while cooler fluid sinks. That density inversion is what sets up convection currents. Denser hot fluid would fall, and the cell would not start.

q: There is an upward buoyant force on the hotter fluid, making it rise while the cooler and denser fluid sinks.
e: True. That cell is a convection current. Natural convection is buoyancy-driven; a fan would be forced convection. Hotter fluid is less dense, so an upward buoyant force lifts it while cooler fluid sinks.

q: Convection occurs only in a liquid or a gas, never in a solid.
e: True. The bulk has to be free to flow. Solids still conduct heat, but that is not convection. Convection occurs only in a liquid or a gas, never in a solid.

q: Convection occurs in solids, liquids, and gases equally.
e: False. Convection occurs only in liquids and gases, never in a solid. A solid cannot flow as a bulk current. Solids still conduct, but that is a different mode.

q: Buoyant force is what drives natural convection.
e: True. No fan is required. Forced convection is when you impose the motion yourself. Hotter fluid is less dense, so an upward buoyant force lifts it while cooler fluid sinks.

q: The basic equation for the rate of convection heat transfer is known as Newton's law of cooling.
e: True. q is the convective coefficient in W m^-2 K^-1. Fourier's name stays with conduction. Newton's law of cooling is the basic convection-rate equation, H = q A (T2 - T1).

q: The basic equation for the rate of convection heat transfer is known as Fourier's law of cooling.
e: False. The convection-rate equation is Newton's law of cooling. Fourier's law is conduction, heat flux against temperature gradient. Mixing the two names swaps solid conduction for fluid cooling.

q: In Newton's law of cooling, $q$ is the convective heat transfer coefficient.
e: True. SI unit is W m^-2 K^-1, one extra metre compared with k. H is then q A Delta T. Newton's law of cooling is the basic convection-rate equation, H = q A (T2 - T1).

q: When $T_2 > T_1$ in convection, heat is gained by the object and $H$ is positive.
e: True. Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Convection is heat carried by the fluid itself as it circulates.

q: When $T_2 < T_1$ in convection, heat is gained by the object and $H$ is positive.
e: False. If the surrounding fluid is colder than the surface, the object loses heat and H is not a gain. Heat is gained when T2 is greater than T1. Sign follows that temperature order.

q: Heat radiation is a transfer of heat that does not require a material medium.
e: True. Radiation transfers heat without a material medium. Electromagnetic waves can cross vacuum. Conduction and convection both need matter.

q: Heat radiation is a transfer of heat that strictly requires a dense material medium.
e: False. Radiation does not require a material medium at all. Electromagnetic waves cross vacuum with no attenuation from matter. Conduction and convection are the modes that need material.

q: Heat is transferred by thermal radiation which are electromagnetic waves that pass through a medium or even vacuum.
e: True. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not attenuate the wave. Mechanical or sound waves are a different family.

q: Energy transfer by radiation is the fastest (at the speed of light) and it suffers no attenuation in a vacuum.
e: True. Sound speed and wind speed are irrelevant here. The wave is electromagnetic. Radiation is the fastest heat transfer, at the speed of light, with no attenuation in vacuum.

q: Energy transfer by radiation suffers maximum attenuation in a vacuum.
e: False. Radiation suffers no attenuation in vacuum and travels at the speed of light. There is nothing in empty space to absorb the wave. Air or glass can weaken it; vacuum does not.

q: Thermal radiation is the form of radiation emitted by bodies because of their temperature.
e: True. Thermal radiation is emitted because of a body's temperature. Every body above absolute zero radiates. X-rays, gamma rays, microwaves and radio are electromagnetic too, but they are not temperature radiation in this sense.

q: All bodies at a temperature above absolute zero emit thermal radiation.
e: True. All bodies above absolute zero emit thermal radiation. There is no thermal glow below 0 K, and nothing lives there. Hotter bodies radiate much more because of the T^4 law.

q: Only bodies at a temperature below absolute zero emit thermal radiation.
e: False. Nothing sits below absolute zero, and every body above 0 K emits thermal radiation. Absolute zero is the floor, not a glow condition. Temperature, not a below-zero fiction, is what drives thermal emission.

q: Thermal radiation differs from other forms of electromagnetic radiation such as X-rays, gamma rays, microwave and radio wave that are not related to temperature.
e: True. Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not attenuate the wave. Thermal radiation is the electromagnetic emission tied to temperature.

q: Radiation is mostly considered to be a surface phenomenon for solids that are opaque to thermal radiation.
e: True. The radiating layer is the surface, not the whole volume. A bulk-volume picture belongs to media that infrared can cross. For solids opaque to thermal radiation, emission is treated as a surface phenomenon.

q: Radiation is mostly considered to be a bulk volume phenomenon for solids that are opaque to thermal radiation.
e: False. For opaque solids, thermal radiation is treated as a surface phenomenon. The emitting layer is the surface, not the whole volume. Volume emission belongs to materials that are not opaque in the infrared.

q: If an object has a good rate of emission of radiation, then it also has a good rate of absorption.
e: True. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not weaken the wave. It travels at the speed of light. Radiation is heat as electromagnetic waves.

q: The object which can absorb all the electromagnetic radiations falling upon it is called a blackbody.
e: True. A blackbody absorbs all electromagnetic radiation that falls on it. It is also the best emitter, with emissivity 1. A perfect reflector is the opposite surface.

q: The object which can reflect all the electromagnetic radiations falling upon it is called a blackbody.
e: False. A blackbody absorbs all radiation that falls on it; it does not reflect all of it. That perfect absorber is also the best emitter. A full reflector is a poor absorber and a poor radiator.

q: The blackbody is not only a perfect absorber but also a best emitter of radiation.
e: True. Emissivity is taken as 1. Real surfaces emit less than this ideal at the same temperature. Radiation is heat as electromagnetic waves.

q: The total emissive power is defined as the total radiant energy of different wavelengths emitted from unit area of a surface of a body in one second.
e: True. Real surfaces emit less, scaled by emissivity. Total emissive power is all wavelengths of radiant energy leaving unit area in one second. For a blackbody it grows as T^4.

q: The total emissive power of a blackbody is directly proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature.
e: True. A blackbody's total emissive power is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature. That is Stefan-Boltzmann's law, e0 = sigma T^4. A square law would be far too weak.

q: The total emissive power of a blackbody is directly proportional to the square of absolute temperature.
e: False. Stefan-Boltzmann's law is a fourth-power law, e0 = sigma T^4, not a square law. Square would understate how fast radiation grows with kelvin. Real surfaces still follow T^4, scaled by emissivity.

q: The equation $e_0 = \sigma T^4$ is known as Stefan-Boltzmann's law.
e: True. Sigma is about 5.685 x 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4. Watch the metre squared, not metre to the minus one. Stefan-Boltzmann's law is e0 = sigma T^4.

q: The radiation emitted by all real surfaces is less than the radiation emitted by a blackbody at the same temperature.
e: True. Every real surface emits less than a blackbody at the same temperature. Emissivity is the ratio of those two powers, at most 1. Greater-than-blackbody emission would break the definition.

q: The radiation emitted by all real surfaces is greater than the radiation emitted by a blackbody at the same temperature.
e: False. Every real surface emits less than a blackbody at the same temperature. Emissivity is at most 1. Greater-than-blackbody emission would break that definition.

q: Emissivity is defined as the ratio of the total emissive power of an object to that of the blackbody, at the same temperature and wavelength.
e: True. Emissivity is the object's total emissive power divided by the blackbody's, at the same temperature and wavelength. Shininess drops that ratio. Dull black sits near 1; polished silver sits near 0.

q: Emissivity of an object depends to a large extent on how shiny it is.
e: True. It also depends on wavelength, so one number is only a first look. Emissivity depends strongly on how shiny the surface is. Shiny metal reflects and radiates poorly.

q: A black object is a good absorber and a good radiator whose emissivity is close to 1.
e: True. A black object is a good absorber and a good radiator, so emissivity is close to 1. White, clear, or silver-coated surfaces sit near 0. Good absorber and good emitter travel together.

q: A white, clear, or silver coated object is a poor absorber and a poor radiator whose emissivity is close to 1.
e: False. A white, clear, or silver-coated object is a poor absorber and a poor radiator, so emissivity is close to 0, not 1. Near 1 is the dull black case. Shininess is what drops emissivity.

q: The net energy change is simply the difference between the radiated energy and the absorbed energy.
e: True. In a colder room it is a net emitter. Net energy change of a radiating body is radiated energy minus absorbed energy. A body in a hotter room absorbs more than it emits and warms up.

q: Thermodynamics is the study of systems involving energy in the form of heat and work.
e: True. Mechanical kinetic energy alone is not the whole subject. Thermodynamics studies systems whose energy appears as heat and work. A piston confining gas in a cylinder is the usual picture.

q: Thermodynamics is the study of systems involving energy exclusively in the form of mechanical kinetic energy.
e: False. Thermodynamics studies heat and work, not mechanical kinetic energy alone. A piston-and-gas cylinder is the usual example. Internal energy includes microscopic motion, not just bulk KE.

q: Thermal equilibrium is an important concept in thermodynamics.
e: True. Maximum heat flow would mean the opposite, a temperature gap. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer, which happens when temperatures match. Zeroth law then lets a thermometer define that shared temperature.

q: When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is no net heat transfer between them.
e: True. Maximum heat flow would mean the opposite, a temperature gap. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer, which happens when temperatures match. Two systems are in thermal equilibrium there cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is maximum net heat transfer between them.
e: False. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer. The two systems already share a temperature. Maximum flow would require a temperature difference.

q: Systems at the same temperature will be in thermal equilibrium with each other.
e: True. Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer, which happens when temperatures match. Zeroth law then lets a thermometer define that shared temperature. Maximum heat flow would mean the opposite, a temperature gap.

q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that when two objects are separately in thermodynamic equilibrium with a third object, they all are in thermodynamic equilibrium with each other.
e: True. Zeroth law: if two objects are each in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. That is how temperature becomes a comparable property. A fourth object is not part of the statement.

q: The first law of thermodynamics is an application of the conservation energy for heat and thermodynamic processes.
e: True. Momentum or mass conservation is a different book. First law is conservation of energy applied to heat and thermodynamic processes. Delta U = Q - W, with W the work done by the system.

q: The first law of thermodynamics relates the change in internal energy of a system to heat added and the work done by the system.
e: True. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead. Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Q is positive when heat is added, negative when heat is removed.

q: The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of a system is equal to the net heat flow $Q$ into the system minus the total work $W$ done by the system.
e: True. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead. Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Change in internal energy Delta U of cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of a system is equal to the net heat flow $Q$ into the system plus the total work $W$ done by the system.
e: False. First law is Delta U = Q minus W, not Q plus W, when W is work done by the system. You subtract the energy the system spends as work. Adding W would count that energy twice.

q: In the first law of thermodynamics, $Q$ is positive if heat is added to the system, and negative if heat is removed.
e: True. The two branches complement each other; they are not unrelated. Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body.

q: In the first law of thermodynamics, $W$ is positive if work is done on the system, and negative if work is done by the system.
e: False. In this sign convention W is positive when the system does work, and negative when work is done on the system. Q is positive when heat is added. Flip those work signs and Delta U = Q - W fails.

q: The internal energy $U$ of a system is defined as the sum of the energies of all the constituent particles.
e: True. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. Internal energy U is the sum of the energies of all constituent particles. For an ideal gas that total tracks absolute temperature only.

q: The internal energy of ideal gases depends only on temperature, not on volume or pressure.
e: True. U is proportional to absolute temperature. An isothermal ideal-gas process therefore has Delta U = 0. Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, not on volume or pressure.

q: The internal energy of ideal gases depends only on volume and pressure, not on temperature.
e: False. An ideal gas stores internal energy by temperature alone, not by volume or pressure. U is proportional to absolute temperature. Change V or p at fixed T and U stays put.

q: Internal energy of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.
e: True. The monoatomic formula is U = (3/2) n R T. Inverse or exponential would not match that kinetic-theory count. Ideal-gas internal energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

q: Heat transfer and work are both energy in transit.
e: True. Heat and work are both energy in transit. Neither is stored as such inside the system. What stays behind is a change in internal energy.

q: Heat transfer and work are both stored as such in a system.
e: False. Heat and work are energy in transit, not stored inventories. What the system stores is internal energy. After the process, you cannot point to a pile of heat or a pile of work inside.

q: Internal energy is a form of energy completely different from either heat or work.
e: True. Heat and work are path-dependent transfers. After the process you can quote U; you cannot quote a leftover pile of heat. Internal energy is a stored state property, different from heat or work.

q: A thermodynamic process may be defined as a change from one equilibrium state of a system to another.
e: True. Quasi-static means you crawl slowly enough to stay in internal equilibrium. A sudden bang is not that ideal path. A thermodynamic process is a change from one equilibrium state to another.

q: In thermodynamics, a quasi-static process is a thermodynamic process that happens slowly enough for the system to remain in internal physical thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: True. You can then draw it as a curve on a p-V diagram and retrace it. Rapid processes jump off that curve. A quasi-static, or quasi-equilibrium, process is slow enough that the system remains in internal thermodynamic equilibrium.

q: In thermodynamics, a quasi-static process is a thermodynamic process that happens very rapidly to prevent the system from remaining in internal physical thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: False. A quasi-static process is slow enough that the system stays in internal equilibrium. Rapid jumps throw it off the equilibrium path. Slow, not fast, is the reversible ideal.

q: An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure.
e: True. Work done by the system is then p Delta V. Constant volume is isochoric, constant temperature is isothermal. Isobaric means constant pressure.

q: An isobaric process occurs at constant volume.
e: False. Isobaric means constant pressure. Constant volume is isochoric. At constant pressure the work is p Delta V.

q: The work done by the system in an isobaric process is simply the pressure multiplied by the change in volume.
e: True. Constant volume is isochoric, constant temperature is isothermal. Isobaric means constant pressure. Work done by the system is then p Delta V.

q: An isochoric process occurs at constant volume.
e: True. For an ideal gas that heat is n Cv Delta T. Isochoric means constant volume, so W = p Delta V = 0. First law then says Delta U equals the heat that entered or left.

q: When the volume of a thermodynamic system is constant, no work is done by the system because $W = p \Delta V = 0$.
e: True. In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Work done on the system is negative W in this convention. Heat added is positive Q.

q: According to the first law, in an isochoric process, the change in internal energy must equal any heat flowing into or out of the system.
e: True. Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Q is positive when heat is added, negative when heat is removed. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead.

q: An isothermal process occurs at a constant temperature.
e: True. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium.

q: For an ideal gas, internal energy $U$ is only a function of the volume.
e: False. For an ideal gas, U is a function of temperature only, not of volume. An isothermal ideal-gas process therefore has Delta U = 0. Volume can change while U stays fixed.

q: Internal energy is constant; therefore, $\Delta U$ is equal to zero for an isothermal process.
e: True. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q.

q: Since $\Delta U = 0$, according to the first law, $W = Q$ for an isothermal process.
e: True. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Since Delta U 0 according to the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: In an adiabatic process, there is no heat transfer into or out of the system, i.e., $Q = 0$.
e: True. Adiabatic means Q = 0, no heat in or out, often by insulating the system. First law collapses to Delta U = -W. Gamma = Cp/Cv then appears in the reversible adiabatic relations.

q: In an adiabatic process, there is maximum heat transfer into or out of the system.
e: False. Adiabatic means Q = 0, no heat in or out. First law then collapses to Delta U = -W. Insulation, not a heat flood, is the adiabatic setup.

q: The first law of thermodynamics $\Delta U = Q - W$ is thus reduced to $\Delta U = -W$ for an adiabatic process.
e: True. Adiabatic means Q = 0, no heat in or out, often by insulating the system. First law collapses to Delta U = -W. First law of thermodynamics Delta U Q cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: An adiabatic process can be done by enclosing the system in a thermal insulator.
e: True. First law collapses to Delta U = -W. Gamma = Cp/Cv then appears in the reversible adiabatic relations. Low thermal conductivity means a poor conductor, a thermal insulator.

q: Heat engine is a system that converts heat to mechanical energy, which can then be used to do mechanical work.
e: True. It repeats a cycle so work keeps coming out. Turning work into heat is dissipation, not this engine. A heat engine converts heat into mechanical energy so it can do mechanical work.

q: Heat engine is a system that converts mechanical energy to heat energy, which can then be used to do thermal work.
e: False. A heat engine converts heat into mechanical energy so that mechanical work can be delivered. The opposite direction is closer to a mechanical dissipater. Cycle after cycle, work is the output.

q: A series of processes in which a system is brought back to its initial state is called a cycle.
e: True. A cycle is a series of processes that returns the system to its initial state. Net Delta U over a cycle is zero. Then W equals Q_H minus Q_C for a heat engine.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ratio of work output to heat input.
e: True. Thermal efficiency is work output over heat input, W/Q_H. You can also write 1 - Q_C/Q_H. Heat input over work output is the reciprocal, not the efficiency.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ratio of heat input to work output.
e: False. Thermal efficiency is work output over heat input, W/Q_H, not the reciprocal. A ratio bigger than 1 would claim more work than the heat you paid. The leftover heat is Q_C.

q: Applying the first law of thermodynamic to one complete cycle, remembering that there is no net change of internal energy ($\Delta U = 0$), we get, $Q_H - Q_C = W$.
e: True. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles.

q: The transformation of heat into work is usually accomplished in practice by two general types of engine; the internal combustion engine and the steam engine.
e: True. In both, a gas in a cylinder is taken around a cycle. Nuclear or solar plants are different textbook chapters. Practical heat-into-work machines are internal combustion engines and steam engines.

q: In the gasoline engines, the combustion of the gasoline and air takes place explosively by an electric spark.
e: True. Diesel instead compresses air only and injects fuel that auto-ignites. A gasoline engine ignites the fuel-air mix with an electric spark. Four of the six processes are piston strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust.

q: In the gasoline engines, the combustion of the gasoline and air takes place slowly by compression heat alone.
e: False. In a gasoline engine the mixture explodes from an electric spark, not from compression heat alone. Slow compression ignition is the diesel idea. Gasoline needs that spark at the end of the compression stroke.

q: The cycle involves the performance of six processes, of which four require motion of the piston and are called strokes.
e: True. A gas confined by a piston in a cylinder is the usual thermodynamic system. Heat in, work out, and U can all be tracked on that cylinder. Strokes are the piston motions in an engine cycle.

q: Intake stroke: A mixture of gasoline vapour and air is drawn into the cylinder by the suction stroke of the piston.
e: True. Diesel intake draws air only. Compression then raises p and T of whatever was drawn in. On the gasoline intake, or suction, stroke the piston draws in gasoline vapour and air.

q: Compression stroke: The mixture of gasoline vapour and air is compressed until its pressure and temperature rise considerably.
e: True. The compression stroke squeezes the charge until pressure and temperature rise sharply. Gasoline then waits for a spark; diesel waits for injected fuel. Volume falls; p and T climb.

q: Explosion: Combustion of the hot mixture is caused to take place very rapidly by an electric spark.
e: True. Gasoline combustion is a rapid spark explosion at nearly constant volume; the piston barely moves in that instant. Pressure jumps, then the power stroke expands the hot gases. Diesel ignition is compression heat plus injection, not that spark pop.

q: Power stroke: The hot combustion products expand and push the piston out, thus suffering a drop in pressure and temperature.
e: True. That is the work-delivery leg. Exhaust then dumps what is left. On the power stroke the hot gases expand, push the piston, and drop in pressure and temperature.

q: Valve exhaust: The combustion products at the end of the power stroke are still at a higher pressure and temperature than the outside.
e: True. Exhaust then dumps what is left. On the power stroke the hot gases expand, push the piston, and drop in pressure and temperature. That is the work-delivery leg.

q: Exhaust stroke: The piston pushes almost all the remaining combustion products out of the cylinder.
e: True. They still leave hotter and at higher pressure than the outside. A slightly larger push than outside pressure is needed to empty the cylinder. The exhaust stroke has the piston push remaining combustion products out.

q: The diesel engine operates on either a two-stroke or four-stroke cycle.
e: True. A full cycle has net Delta U = 0, so W = Q_H - Q_C. A diesel draws only air, then sprays fuel that ignites from compression heat and pressure. No spark is required at that instant.

q: Unlike the spark-ignition gasoline engine, the diesel engine induces only air into the combustion chamber on its intake stroke.
e: True. Four of the six processes are piston strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Diesel instead compresses air only and injects fuel that auto-ignites. On the gasoline intake, or suction, stroke the piston draws in gasoline vapour and air.

q: Unlike the spark-ignition gasoline engine, the diesel engine induces a mixture of fuel and air into the combustion chamber on its intake stroke.
e: False. A diesel draws only air on the intake stroke. Fuel is sprayed in later and ignites from the heat and pressure. The gasoline engine is the one that intakes a fuel-air mixture.

q: Diesel fuel is sprayed into the cylinder by the injector and immediately ignites because of the heat and pressure inside the cylinder.
e: True. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. A diesel draws only air, then sprays fuel that ignites from compression heat and pressure. No spark is required at that instant.

q: In 1824, Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical engine known as Carnot engine.
e: True. In 1824 Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical reversible engine between two reservoirs. That Carnot engine sets the upper efficiency bound for every real engine on the same pair of temperatures. Friction and irreversibility make real engines worse.

q: Carnot engine is a heat engine operates on an ideal reversible cycle (Carnot cycle) between two heat reservoirs.
e: True. It is an upper limit, not a workshop motor. All reversible engines on that pair share the same efficiency. The Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats between two reservoirs.

q: Carnot engine is a heat engine operates on an irreversible cycle between two heat reservoirs.
e: False. The Carnot engine runs on an ideal reversible cycle between two reservoirs. Irreversibility is what makes real engines worse. Two isotherms and two adiabats, all reversible, make the Carnot loop.

q: Carnot engine sets an upper limit on the efficiency of all other real engines.
e: True. You must use absolute temperatures in eta_c = 1 - T_C/T_H. Real cycles leak heat and generate friction, so they sit below that ceiling. Carnot sets an upper limit on the efficiency of steam, gasoline and diesel engines between the same temperatures.

q: All real engines are less efficient than Carnot engine because they do not operate through a reversible cycle.
e: True. All reversible engines on that pair share the same efficiency. The Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats between two reservoirs. It is an upper limit, not a workshop motor.

q: All real engines are more efficient than Carnot engine because they operate through a reversible cycle.
e: False. Real engines are less efficient than Carnot, because they are not reversible and they lose energy to friction and conduction. Carnot sets the upper bound. Nobody beats that bound between the same two reservoirs.

q: In a reversible process, the system undergoing the process can be returned to its initial condition along the same path on the p-V diagram.
e: True. In a reversible process you can return along the same p-V path to the start. Infinitesimally slow is the main thermodynamic condition. An irreversible process cannot retrace that path.

q: The most important condition for a process to be reversible in thermodynamics is that the process should be carried out infinitesimally slowly.
e: True. The two branches complement each other; they are not unrelated. A reversible process can retrace the same p-V path if you go infinitesimally slowly. Carnot's four legs are all reversible.

q: The most important condition for a process to be reversible in thermodynamics is that the process should be carried out as rapidly as possible.
e: False. Reversibility wants the process carried out infinitesimally slowly, so the system can retrace the same p-V path. Rush it and you leave equilibrium. Rapid is the irreversible direction.

q: The Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes; two isothermal processes and two adiabatic processes.
e: True. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case.

q: The Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes; two isobaric processes and two isochoric processes.
e: False. The Carnot cycle is two reversible isotherms and two reversible adiabats. Isobaric and isochoric legs belong to other model cycles. Those four Carnot legs are what set the T_C/T_H efficiency.

q: Carnot's theorem states that no engine operating between two heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: True. Carnot's theorem: no engine between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine on those reservoirs. The corollary is that all reversible engines on that pair are equally efficient. Different efficiencies mean irreversibility or different temperatures.

q: Carnot's theorem states that any engine operating between two heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: False. Carnot's theorem forbids any engine between two reservoirs from beating Carnot on those same reservoirs. More efficient than Carnot would break the second-law bound. Reversible engines on that pair are equally efficient, not wilder.

q: A corollary to Carnot's theorem states that all reversible engines operating between the same heat reservoirs are equally efficient.
e: True. The corollary is that all reversible engines on that pair are equally efficient. Different efficiencies mean irreversibility or different temperatures. Carnot's theorem: no engine between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine on those reservoirs.

q: A corollary to Carnot's theorem states that all reversible engines operating between the same heat reservoirs have different efficiencies.
e: False. The corollary is that all reversible engines between the same reservoirs are equally efficient. Different efficiencies would appear only if the engines were irreversible or the reservoirs differed. Carnot's value is shared, not scattered.
